The world's largest desalination plant is located in **Saudi Arabia**.

Specifically, it is the **Ras Al-Khair Power and Desalination Plant**, which holds the Guinness World Record as the world's largest hybrid water desalination plant. Key details about the plant include:
*   **Location:** Ras Al-Khair on the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia (near Jubail).
*   **Capacity:** It has a production capacity of approximately 1.036 million cubic meters (m³) of water per day (some sources round this to over 1 billion liters per day).
*   **Technology:** It uses a hybrid system combining thermal multistage flash (MSF) distillation and reverse osmosis (RO), alongside power generation capabilities (2,400 MW).
*   **Operational Date:** It began operations in April 2014.

It is worth noting that while Ras Al-Khair is the largest *overall* hybrid plant, the **Taweelah** plant in the UAE is often cited as the largest *reverse osmosis (RO)-only* plant globally with a capacity of about 909,000 m³/day. However, in terms of total combined output, Saudi Arabia's Ras Al-Khair remains the top-ranked facility.

Title: Desalination Plants: Ten of the World's Largest

The recently awarded Rabigh 3 desalination project in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to ACWA Power was branded as one of the world’s largest desalination plants.
To put it into perspective, with a capacity of 600,000 m3/day, that’s 600 million litres of water that will eventually be produced per day.
There is no doubting at that size, the Saudi mega-size project will be one of the largest out there and the second largest awarded RO desalination plant.
Yet most desalination professionals will know it’s not _the_ largest and it raises the question of well, with over 20,000 desalination plants contracted around the world, which are the largest?
We set out to put together this top ten list.
1.   ### Ras Al Khair, Saudi Arabia: 1,036,000 m3/day
Commonly regarded as the desalination heavyweight of the world, the massive Ras Al-Khair is a hybrid project that uses both thermal multistage flash (MSF) and reverse osmosis (RO) technologies.
Located 75km north-west of Jubail and serving Riyadh, the site also has a substantial power generation component, with a capacity of 2,400MW.
The main contractor for plant construction was Doosan and its consortium partner Saudi Archirodon, with Poyry acting as the consultant for the project.
Ras Al-Khair started operations in 2014 but in 2017 was put up for sale by the Saline Water Conversion Corporation (SWCC) to kickstart privatisation plans and the sale of its assets.
2.   ### Taweelah, UAE – 909,200 m3/day
Despite the project being in its infancy, when complete Taweelah will catapult the UAE into the top three list.
To date, seven consortia are bidding on the mega project, including: ACWA Power; Suez International Power SA Dubai Branch (Engie), with Marubeni Corp; Sumitomo Corp, with Veolia Middle East; Valoriza Agua, with Utico FZC and IDB Infrastructure Fund II; Cobra Instalaciones y Servicios, with Orascom Construction; Acciona Agua, with Pal Group; and Suez International, with Sojitz Corporation and NV Besix SA.

ACWA Power with EPC consortium comprising Sepco3 and Abengoa has so far placed the lowest bid using the higher electricity tariff at AED8.26 ($2.25) at $0.49 per cubic metre.
More than 40 companies were reported to have initially shown interest in the Taweelah tender.
Once complete, the Taweela power and water complete is expected to raise the emirate’s proportion of desalinated produced water by RO from 13 percent today to 30 percent by 2022.
3.   ### Shuaiba 3, Saudi Arabia – 880,000 m3/day
A second in the list for Saudi Arabia, the Shuaiba 3 development is located 90 kilometres south of the historic city of Jeddah.
A consortium involving Siemens of Germany for the power plant and Doosan for the thermal desalination plant were selected by ACWA Power to provide project engineering, procurement and construction of the plant.
One expansion to the plant has been completed and one expansion is in the final construction stage with a total additional 400,000 m3/day of RO capacity added, according to ACWA Power.
When complete in the first half of 2019, Shuaiba will eventually overtake Ras Al Khair as the largest operating desalination plant with total capacity of 1,282,000 m3/day.
The development is part of wider plans from the Water and Electricity Company (WEC) to significantly increase desalination capacity in the country.
4.   ### Jubail Water and Power Company (JWAP), Saudi Arabia - 800,000 m3 /day
One of the world’s most notable integrated water and power facilities (IWPP), the Jubail Plant is a joint venture between Marafiq, Saudi Electricity Company (SEC), the Water and Electricity Holding Company, and the SGA Marafiq Consortium comprising ENGIE, Gulf Investment Corporation, and ACWA Power Projects.
Commercial operation started at the end of 2010 with a 20-year period slated term for operation. A dual-purpose facility, JWAP includes combined-cycle based power and multi-effect distillation (MED) water generation.

The plant is split into four operational blocks. Three of the four blocks are power and desalination blocks, each of which comprises three gas turbines operating in a combined cycle with a single back pressure steam turbine feeding each nine desalination MED units. The fourth block is a ‘power only’ block with three gas turbines a one reheat condensing steam turbine.
The plant is owned by Jubail Water and Power Company (JWAP). The off-taker is Marafiq Water and Supply Company (Tawreed), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Marafiq, which purchases all of the plant output through a 20-year Power and Water Purchase Agreement (PWPA) with JWAP.
5.   ### Umm Al Quwain (UAQ), UAE – 682,900 m3/day
_Image credit: Sidem Veolia_  
Based in the Emirate of Umm Al Quwain and along the border of Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, the independent water project (IWP) is one of the largest pure play reverse osmosis plants in the listing.
Expected to be commercially operational in the third quarter of 2022, UAQ is being delivered as a build, own, operate and transfer (BOOT) with a water purchase agreement (WPA) term of 35 years, with the Federal Electricity and Water Authority (FEWA) as the off-taker.
The US$797 million project is being constructed by Chinese partner, Gezhouba Group International Engineering, with SIDEM-Veolia delivering the US$255 million engineering and procurement contract. ACWA Power will have a 40 per cent share, with Techton Engineering and Construction 35 per cent.
6.   ### DEWA Station M, Dubai - 636,000 m3/day
The Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) M-Station project is one of the largest power and desalination plants in UAE, producing 636,600 m3/day of potable water and with a total power capacity of 2,885MW.

The project has been implemented in phases since mid-2010. Completed in 2012, the desalination plant was built in eight units by Italian company, FisiaItalimpianti. Multi-Stage Flash (MSF) distillation technology is used, each with a capacity of 80,000 m3/day.
The combined total cost of the construction and expansion of M-Station, equipped with the latest smart devices and sophisticated heavy-duty technological systems, is AED11.5 billion (US$3.1bn).
Furthermore, two dual-fuel-fired auxiliary boilers of 390 tons per hour, and 16 fuel-oil storage tanks, each with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters, with total fuel-oil storage of 320,000 cubic metres.
7.   ### Sorek, Israel – 624,000 m3/day
If Ras Al Khair is considered the heavyweight hybrid of the world then Sorek should be considered the heavyweight membrane plant of the world in operation with an enormous 624,000 m3/day capacity.
Located 15km south of Tel Aviv in Israel and developed by IDE Technologies, the project was and continues to be unique in the use of 16 inch seawater reverse osmosis membranes but in a vertical formation.
A further development – Sorek 2 – has since been announced with a capacity of 548,000 m3/day. A total of **seven local and international companies were recently shortlisted to develop the project.**
Once complete, Sorek 2 will be the sixth desalination plant to operate in Israel alongside Hadera, Ashkelon, the first Sorek, Palmachim and Ashdod.
8.   ### Jubail 3A IWP, Saudi Arabia - 600,000 m3/day
With an investment value of US$650 million, the Jubail 3A Independent Water Plant (IWP) will generate 600,000 m3/day of potable water.
The greenfield seawater reverse osmosis desalination project is set for commercial operation in the fourth quarter of 2022.

The **Ras Al-Khair Power and Desalination Plant** is a power and desalination plant located in Ras Al-Khair on the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia. It is operated by the Saline Water Conversion Corporation of Saudi Arabia. The plant began operating in April 2014 and, as of January 2017, is the world's largest hybrid water desalination plant.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-StartsPumping-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-2) The project includes a power plant capable of producing 2400 MW of electricity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-StartsPumping-1) In 2015, it won the Global Water Awards "Desalination Plant of the Year" award.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-4)
Construction of the plant began in 2011.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5) Though originally slated to begin producing freshwater by the end of 2013,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-6) the first freshwater produced from the plant was in early 2015.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-Bennett2-7) Full commercial operation of the plant was achieved in March 2016.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-8)

The primary contractors for construction of the plant were the Doosan Group and Saudi Archirodon.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5) Doosan was awarded the prime contract in September, 2010.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-Bennett1-9) Additional contractors for the plant included Fluid Equipment Development Company for energy recovery devices, Siemens for generators, turbines, and related equipment, and Hyosung for various motors.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5)
The plant has created 3,500 direct and indirect jobs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-StartsPumping-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-10)

Water intake for the plant comes from the Persian Gulf, on the shore of which the plant sits.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5) The plant includes five high-efficiency gas turbines operated in combined cycle mode and in single mode.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5) It uses a hybrid system of eight multi-stage flashing units and 17 reverse osmosis units.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-11) Freshwater output from the plant is pumped via pipelines to Riyadh and Hafr Al-Batin.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-StartsPumping-1) Electricity and freshwater output from the plant also supply a nearby aluminium oxide refinery.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5) Of the 2400 MW electricity produced by the plant, 200 MW are used by the plant itself.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-Bennett2-7)Effluent from the plant is processed locally by a dedicated wastewater treatment plant and discharged into the Persian Gulf.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al-Khair_Power_and_Desalination_Plant#cite_note-WaterTechnology-5)

Is Water — Not Oil — the Real Strategic Vulnerability in the Middle East? While global attention remains fixed on oil supply chains, maritime routes and geopolitical escalation, a far more fragile asset underpins the survival of Gulf economies: desalinated water. Consider the scale: • The Middle East accounts for ~50% of the world’s desalination capacity. • Countries like Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain rely on desalination for 70–100% of their potable water supply. • Saudi Arabia alone produces over 7 million m³/day of desalinated water. • Major coastal cities — Riyadh (via long transmission lines), Jeddah, Dammam, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha — are structurally dependent on these plants. Unlike oil, water cannot be stockpiled in strategic reserves at meaningful urban scale. Unlike electricity, it cannot be imported instantly across borders. Unlike fuel, it cannot be substituted. Most desalination plants in the Gulf are located along coastlines and are energy-intensive, grid-dependent, and networked through large transmission corridors. Any disruption — whether targeted or collateral — could have cascading effects within 48–72 hours in dense urban centres. If desalination infrastructure were damaged — intentionally or accidentally — the humanitarian consequences would be immediate. Water systems cannot be quickly replaced, rerouted or improvised. A single major disruption could impact entire metropolitan populations within days. This is not theoretical. Having worked as a technocrat at the Yanbu Power Plant–cum–Desalination facility in Saudi Arabia on behalf of Kuljian Corporation (USA), serving as Project Consultant to the Saudi Water Conservation Company (SWCC), I have seen first-hand: • The scale of multi-stage flash (MSF) and reverse osmosis systems • The energy-water nexus dependency • The logistical complexity of long-distance transmission pipelines • The limited buffer storage available relative to population demand In hyper-arid regions where annual rainfall is negligible and renewable freshwater resources are minimal, desalination is not infrastructure — it is existential security. A prolonged outage of even one mega plant could: • Disrupt municipal supply to millions • Halt industrial production • Affect healthcare systems • Trigger emergency rationing • Create humanitarian stress within days Beyond geopolitics lies a fundamental systems reality: Oil drives economies. Water sustains civilizations.

The recently awarded Rabigh 3 desalination project in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to ACWA Power was branded as one of the world’s largest desalination plants.
To put it into perspective, with a capacity of 600,000 m3/day, that’s 600 million litres of water that will eventually be produced per day.
There is no doubting at that size, the Saudi mega-size project will be one of the largest out there and the second largest awarded RO desalination plant.
Yet most desalination professionals will know it’s not _the_ largest and it raises the question of well, with over 20,000 desalination plants contracted around the world, which are the largest?
We set out to put together this top ten list.
1.   ### Ras Al Khair, Saudi Arabia: 1,036,000 m3/day
Commonly regarded as the desalination heavyweight of the world, the massive Ras Al-Khair is a hybrid project that uses both thermal multistage flash (MSF) and reverse osmosis (RO) technologies.
Located 75km north-west of Jubail and serving Riyadh, the site also has a substantial power generation component, with a capacity of 2,400MW.
The main contractor for plant construction was Doosan and its consortium partner Saudi Archirodon, with Poyry acting as the consultant for the project.
Ras Al-Khair started operations in 2014 but in 2017 was put up for sale by the Saline Water Conversion Corporation (SWCC) to kickstart privatisation plans and the sale of its assets.
2.   ### Taweelah, UAE – 909,200 m3/day
Despite the project being in its infancy, when complete Taweelah will catapult the UAE into the top three list.
To date, seven consortia are bidding on the mega project, including: ACWA Power; Suez International Power SA Dubai Branch (Engie), with Marubeni Corp; Sumitomo Corp, with Veolia Middle East; Valoriza Agua, with Utico FZC and IDB Infrastructure Fund II; Cobra Instalaciones y Servicios, with Orascom Construction; Acciona Agua, with Pal Group; and Suez International, with Sojitz Corporation and NV Besix SA.
texts.1:
ACWA Power with EPC consortium comprising Sepco3 and Abengoa has so far placed the lowest bid using the higher electricity tariff at AED8.26 ($2.25) at $0.49 per cubic metre.
More than 40 companies were reported to have initially shown interest in the Taweelah tender.
Once complete, the Taweela power and water complete is expected to raise the emirate’s proportion of desalinated produced water by RO from 13 percent today to 30 percent by 2022.
3.   ### Shuaiba 3, Saudi Arabia – 880,000 m3/day
A second in the list for Saudi Arabia, the Shuaiba 3 development is located 90 kilometres south of the historic city of Jeddah.
A consortium involving Siemens of Germany for the power plant and Doosan for the thermal desalination plant were selected by ACWA Power to provide project engineering, procurement and construction of the plant.
One expansion to the plant has been completed and one expansion is in the final construction stage with a total additional 400,000 m3/day of RO capacity added, according to ACWA Power.
When complete in the first half of 2019, Shuaiba will eventually overtake Ras Al Khair as the largest operating desalination plant with total capacity of 1,282,000 m3/day.
The development is part of wider plans from the Water and Electricity Company (WEC) to significantly increase desalination capacity in the country.
4.   ### Jubail Water and Power Company (JWAP), Saudi Arabia - 800,000 m3 /day
One of the world’s most notable integrated water and power facilities (IWPP), the Jubail Plant is a joint venture between Marafiq, Saudi Electricity Company (SEC), the Water and Electricity Holding Company, and the SGA Marafiq Consortium comprising ENGIE, Gulf Investment Corporation, and ACWA Power Projects.
Commercial operation started at the end of 2010 with a 20-year period slated term for operation. A dual-purpose facility, JWAP includes combined-cycle based power and multi-effect distillation (MED) water generation.
texts.2:
The plant is split into four operational blocks. Three of the four blocks are power and desalination blocks, each of which comprises three gas turbines operating in a combined cycle with a single back pressure steam turbine feeding each nine desalination MED units. The fourth block is a ‘power only’ block with three gas turbines a one reheat condensing steam turbine.
The plant is owned by Jubail Water and Power Company (JWAP). The off-taker is Marafiq Water and Supply Company (Tawreed), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Marafiq, which purchases all of the plant output through a 20-year Power and Water Purchase Agreement (PWPA) with JWAP.
5.   ### Umm Al Quwain (UAQ), UAE – 682,900 m3/day
_Image credit: Sidem Veolia_  
Based in the Emirate of Umm Al Quwain and along the border of Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, the independent water project (IWP) is one of the largest pure play reverse osmosis plants in the listing.
Expected to be commercially operational in the third quarter of 2022, UAQ is being delivered as a build, own, operate and transfer (BOOT) with a water purchase agreement (WPA) term of 35 years, with the Federal Electricity and Water Authority (FEWA) as the off-taker.
The US$797 million project is being constructed by Chinese partner, Gezhouba Group International Engineering, with SIDEM-Veolia delivering the US$255 million engineering and procurement contract. ACWA Power will have a 40 per cent share, with Techton Engineering and Construction 35 per cent.
6.   ### DEWA Station M, Dubai - 636,000 m3/day
The Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) M-Station project is one of the largest power and desalination plants in UAE, producing 636,600 m3/day of potable water and with a total power capacity of 2,885MW.
texts.3:
The project has been implemented in phases since mid-2010. Completed in 2012, the desalination plant was built in eight units by Italian company, FisiaItalimpianti. Multi-Stage Flash (MSF) distillation technology is used, each with a capacity of 80,000 m3/day.
The combined total cost of the construction and expansion of M-Station, equipped with the latest smart devices and sophisticated heavy-duty technological systems, is AED11.5 billion (US$3.1bn).
Furthermore, two dual-fuel-fired auxiliary boilers of 390 tons per hour, and 16 fuel-oil storage tanks, each with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters, with total fuel-oil storage of 320,000 cubic metres.
7.   ### Sorek, Israel – 624,000 m3/day
If Ras Al Khair is considered the heavyweight hybrid of the world then Sorek should be considered the heavyweight membrane plant of the world in operation with an enormous 624,000 m3/day capacity.
Located 15km south of Tel Aviv in Israel and developed by IDE Technologies, the project was and continues to be unique in the use of 16 inch seawater reverse osmosis membranes but in a vertical formation.
A further development – Sorek 2 – has since been announced with a capacity of 548,000 m3/day. A total of **seven local and international companies were recently shortlisted to develop the project.**
Once complete, Sorek 2 will be the sixth desalination plant to operate in Israel alongside Hadera, Ashkelon, the first Sorek, Palmachim and Ashdod.
8.   ### Jubail 3A IWP, Saudi Arabia - 600,000 m3/day
With an investment value of US$650 million, the Jubail 3A Independent Water Plant (IWP) will generate 600,000 m3/day of potable water.
The greenfield seawater reverse osmosis desalination project is set for commercial operation in the fourth quarter of 2022.

Is Water — Not Oil — the Real Strategic Vulnerability in the Middle East? While global attention remains fixed on oil supply chains, maritime routes and geopolitical escalation, a far more fragile asset underpins the survival of Gulf economies: desalinated water. Consider the scale: • The Middle East accounts for ~50% of the world’s desalination capacity. • Countries like Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain rely on desalination for 70–100% of their potable water supply. • Saudi Arabia alone produces over 7 million m³/day of desalinated water. • Major coastal cities — Riyadh (via long transmission lines), Jeddah, Dammam, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha — are structurally dependent on these plants. Unlike oil, water cannot be stockpiled in strategic reserves at meaningful urban scale. Unlike electricity, it cannot be imported instantly across borders. Unlike fuel, it cannot be substituted. Most desalination plants in the Gulf are located along coastlines and are energy-intensive, grid-dependent, and networked through large transmission corridors. Any disruption — whether targeted or collateral — could have cascading effects within 48–72 hours in dense urban centres. If desalination infrastructure were damaged — intentionally or accidentally — the humanitarian consequences would be immediate. Water systems cannot be quickly replaced, rerouted or improvised. A single major disruption could impact entire metropolitan populations within days. This is not theoretical. Having worked as a technocrat at the Yanbu Power Plant–cum–Desalination facility in Saudi Arabia on behalf of Kuljian Corporation (USA), serving as Project Consultant to the Saudi Water Conservation Company (SWCC), I have seen first-hand: • The scale of multi-stage flash (MSF) and reverse osmosis systems • The energy-water nexus dependency • The logistical complexity of long-distance transmission pipelines • The limited buffer storage available relative to population demand In hyper-arid regions where annual rainfall is negligible and renewable freshwater resources are minimal, desalination is not infrastructure — it is existential security. A prolonged outage of even one mega plant could: • Disrupt municipal supply to millions • Halt industrial production • Affect healthcare systems • Trigger emergency rationing • Create humanitarian stress within days Beyond geopolitics lies a fundamental systems reality: Oil drives economies. Water sustains civilizations.

The recently awarded Rabigh 3 desalination project in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to ACWA Power was branded as one of the world’s largest desalination plants.
To put it into perspective, with a capacity of 600,000 m3/day, that’s 600 million litres of water that will eventually be produced per day.
There is no doubting at that size, the Saudi mega-size project will be one of the largest out there and the second largest awarded RO desalination plant.
Yet most desalination professionals will know it’s not _the_ largest and it raises the question of well, with over 20,000 desalination plants contracted around the world, which are the largest?
We set out to put together this top ten list.
1.   ### Ras Al Khair, Saudi Arabia: 1,036,000 m3/day
Commonly regarded as the desalination heavyweight of the world, the massive Ras Al-Khair is a hybrid project that uses both thermal multistage flash (MSF) and reverse osmosis (RO) technologies.
Located 75km north-west of Jubail and serving Riyadh, the site also has a substantial power generation component, with a capacity of 2,400MW.
The main contractor for plant construction was Doosan and its consortium partner Saudi Archirodon, with Poyry acting as the consultant for the project.
Ras Al-Khair started operations in 2014 but in 2017 was put up for sale by the Saline Water Conversion Corporation (SWCC) to kickstart privatisation plans and the sale of its assets.
2.   ### Taweelah, UAE – 909,200 m3/day
Despite the project being in its infancy, when complete Taweelah will catapult the UAE into the top three list.
To date, seven consortia are bidding on the mega project, including: ACWA Power; Suez International Power SA Dubai Branch (Engie), with Marubeni Corp; Sumitomo Corp, with Veolia Middle East; Valoriza Agua, with Utico FZC and IDB Infrastructure Fund II; Cobra Instalaciones y Servicios, with Orascom Construction; Acciona Agua, with Pal Group; and Suez International, with Sojitz Corporation and NV Besix SA.

ACWA Power with EPC consortium comprising Sepco3 and Abengoa has so far placed the lowest bid using the higher electricity tariff at AED8.26 ($2.25) at $0.49 per cubic metre.
More than 40 companies were reported to have initially shown interest in the Taweelah tender.
Once complete, the Taweela power and water complete is expected to raise the emirate’s proportion of desalinated produced water by RO from 13 percent today to 30 percent by 2022.
3.   ### Shuaiba 3, Saudi Arabia – 880,000 m3/day
A second in the list for Saudi Arabia, the Shuaiba 3 development is located 90 kilometres south of the historic city of Jeddah.
A consortium involving Siemens of Germany for the power plant and Doosan for the thermal desalination plant were selected by ACWA Power to provide project engineering, procurement and construction of the plant.
One expansion to the plant has been completed and one expansion is in the final construction stage with a total additional 400,000 m3/day of RO capacity added, according to ACWA Power.
When complete in the first half of 2019, Shuaiba will eventually overtake Ras Al Khair as the largest operating desalination plant with total capacity of 1,282,000 m3/day.
The development is part of wider plans from the Water and Electricity Company (WEC) to significantly increase desalination capacity in the country.
4.   ### Jubail Water and Power Company (JWAP), Saudi Arabia - 800,000 m3 /day
One of the world’s most notable integrated water and power facilities (IWPP), the Jubail Plant is a joint venture between Marafiq, Saudi Electricity Company (SEC), the Water and Electricity Holding Company, and the SGA Marafiq Consortium comprising ENGIE, Gulf Investment Corporation, and ACWA Power Projects.
Commercial operation started at the end of 2010 with a 20-year period slated term for operation. A dual-purpose facility, JWAP includes combined-cycle based power and multi-effect distillation (MED) water generation.

The plant is split into four operational blocks. Three of the four blocks are power and desalination blocks, each of which comprises three gas turbines operating in a combined cycle with a single back pressure steam turbine feeding each nine desalination MED units. The fourth block is a ‘power only’ block with three gas turbines a one reheat condensing steam turbine.
The plant is owned by Jubail Water and Power Company (JWAP). The off-taker is Marafiq Water and Supply Company (Tawreed), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Marafiq, which purchases all of the plant output through a 20-year Power and Water Purchase Agreement (PWPA) with JWAP.
5.   ### Umm Al Quwain (UAQ), UAE – 682,900 m3/day
_Image credit: Sidem Veolia_  
Based in the Emirate of Umm Al Quwain and along the border of Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, the independent water project (IWP) is one of the largest pure play reverse osmosis plants in the listing.
Expected to be commercially operational in the third quarter of 2022, UAQ is being delivered as a build, own, operate and transfer (BOOT) with a water purchase agreement (WPA) term of 35 years, with the Federal Electricity and Water Authority (FEWA) as the off-taker.
The US$797 million project is being constructed by Chinese partner, Gezhouba Group International Engineering, with SIDEM-Veolia delivering the US$255 million engineering and procurement contract. ACWA Power will have a 40 per cent share, with Techton Engineering and Construction 35 per cent.
6.   ### DEWA Station M, Dubai - 636,000 m3/day
The Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) M-Station project is one of the largest power and desalination plants in UAE, producing 636,600 m3/day of potable water and with a total power capacity of 2,885MW.

The project has been implemented in phases since mid-2010. Completed in 2012, the desalination plant was built in eight units by Italian company, FisiaItalimpianti. Multi-Stage Flash (MSF) distillation technology is used, each with a capacity of 80,000 m3/day.
The combined total cost of the construction and expansion of M-Station, equipped with the latest smart devices and sophisticated heavy-duty technological systems, is AED11.5 billion (US$3.1bn).
Furthermore, two dual-fuel-fired auxiliary boilers of 390 tons per hour, and 16 fuel-oil storage tanks, each with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters, with total fuel-oil storage of 320,000 cubic metres.
7.   ### Sorek, Israel – 624,000 m3/day
If Ras Al Khair is considered the heavyweight hybrid of the world then Sorek should be considered the heavyweight membrane plant of the world in operation with an enormous 624,000 m3/day capacity.
Located 15km south of Tel Aviv in Israel and developed by IDE Technologies, the project was and continues to be unique in the use of 16 inch seawater reverse osmosis membranes but in a vertical formation.
A further development – Sorek 2 – has since been announced with a capacity of 548,000 m3/day. A total of **seven local and international companies were recently shortlisted to develop the project.**
Once complete, Sorek 2 will be the sixth desalination plant to operate in Israel alongside Hadera, Ashkelon, the first Sorek, Palmachim and Ashdod.
8.   ### Jubail 3A IWP, Saudi Arabia - 600,000 m3/day
With an investment value of US$650 million, the Jubail 3A Independent Water Plant (IWP) will generate 600,000 m3/day of potable water.
The greenfield seawater reverse osmosis desalination project is set for commercial operation in the fourth quarter of 2022.

Is Water — Not Oil — the Real Strategic Vulnerability in the Middle East? While global attention remains fixed on oil supply chains, maritime routes and geopolitical escalation, a far more fragile asset underpins the survival of Gulf economies: desalinated water. Consider the scale: • The Middle East accounts for ~50% of the world’s desalination capacity. • Countries like Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain rely on desalination for 70–100% of their potable water supply. • Saudi Arabia alone produces over 7 million m³/day of desalinated water. • Major coastal cities — Riyadh (via long transmission lines), Jeddah, Dammam, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha — are structurally dependent on these plants. Unlike oil, water cannot be stockpiled in strategic reserves at meaningful urban scale. Unlike electricity, it cannot be imported instantly across borders. Unlike fuel, it cannot be substituted. Most desalination plants in the Gulf are located along coastlines and are energy-intensive, grid-dependent, and networked through large transmission corridors. Any disruption — whether targeted or collateral — could have cascading effects within 48–72 hours in dense urban centres. If desalination infrastructure were damaged — intentionally or accidentally — the humanitarian consequences would be immediate. Water systems cannot be quickly replaced, rerouted or improvised.
